tracks.text: Four friends are sharing one hour on a games console.
At first, one turn is much longer than the others.
That is not a fair quarter.
When the four turns become equal, each person gets one of four equal parts of the hour.
The full hour is the whole.
Split it into four equal turns.
Now select one turn.
That is one out of four equal parts, which we write as 1/4 and call one quarter.
Here is a new whole with six equal parts.

Look at all six equal parts.
That total goes on the bottom of the fraction.

First one.
Then two.
Then three.

Check that the four parts are equal, then count the highlighted parts.

Check that the parts are equal.

Counting four regions is not enough.
Compare their sizes before you decide whether they are quarters.

Half of this short bar and half of this longer bar are both one half.

Alright, your turn.

Read the model and write the fraction without any labels from me.
You have got the idea.
Here are five quick questions with different-looking wholes.

Put 1 over 6.

That is it — 3 highlighted parts out of 4 equal parts gives 3/4.
Count all the equal parts for the bottom number.
Count only highlighted parts for the top number.
There are 3 highlighted parts out of 4 equal parts.
Put 3 over 4.

Right — quarters must be equal, so these regions are not quarters.

One region is larger, so the 4 regions are not equal and cannot be quarters.
Yes — 4 coloured boxes out of 10 equal boxes gives 4/10.
Count every box for the bottom number, then count the coloured boxes for the top number.
There are 4 coloured boxes out of 10 equal boxes.
Write 4 over 10.
The whole has 10 equal boxes.
Four are coloured, so the fraction is 4/10.
Exactly — 5 blue counters out of 12 counters gives 5/12.
Treat all 12 counters as the whole.
Count only the blue counters for the top number.
Five counters are blue out of 12 altogether.
Write 5 over 12.
The whole set has 12 counters and 5 are blue, so the fraction is 5/12.
You have it — 7 iced cupcakes out of 9 gives 7/9.
All 9 cupcakes make the whole.
The iced cupcakes give the top number.
Seven of the 9 cupcakes have icing.
Write 7 over 9.
There are 9 cupcakes altogether and 7 have icing, so the fraction is 7/9.
Nice — 2 shaded strips out of 5 equal strips gives 2/5.
Count every strip for the bottom number and only the shaded strips for the top number.
Two of the 5 equal strips are shaded.
Write 2 over 5.
The whole has 5 equal strips and 2 are shaded, so the fraction is 2/5.
Correct — 3 red tiles out of 8 tiles gives 3/8.
All 8 tiles make the whole.
Count the red tiles for the top number.
There are 3 red tiles out of 8 altogether.
Write 3 over 8.
The whole has 8 tiles and 3 are red, so the fraction is 3/8.

Keep 12 on the bottom because the original bar is the whole.
Now work out how many pieces remain.
Twelve minus 5 leaves 7 pieces.
Write 7 over the original 12.
The whole began with 12 equal pieces.
After 5 are eaten, 7 remain, so the fraction is 7/12.
Exactly — sixths must be equal, so these unequal slices are not sixths.
Sixths must be the same size.
Compare the slices before deciding.
The slices are unequal, so each slice cannot be one sixth.
A sixth is one of 6 equal parts.

Ten minus 7 leaves 3 unused lengths.
Write 3 over 10.
The ribbon has 10 equal lengths.
Seven are used, leaving 3, so the unused fraction is 3/10.

One piece is shaded out of 4 equal pieces.
Write 1 over 4.
